title: Quality assessment and grading of onions are often subjective and vary across procurement centers, resulting in disputes and inconsistencies.
org: Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution
description:
Expected Solution: Develop an AI-based mobile application that:
• Uses image processing to assess onion quality.
• Identifies damaged, rotten, sprouted, or undersized onions.
• Estimates Grade A and URS percentages.
• Generates a digital quality report instantly.
• Reduces human bias and improves transparency.
summary: Innovation (3/5): draws on ai applied to a fitness & sports problem, placing it in the moderate band. Feasibility (4/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a working prototype is realistic in a 36-hour window. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Fitness & Sports. Tech Depth (2/5): centers on moderate engineering scope. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 16/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: AI-Based Quality Assessment and Grading System for Onions at Procurement Centers

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a mobile app that photographs onions and automatically grades their quality, catching damaged, rotten, or undersized ones, so procurement centers get consistent, fair grading instead of one inspector's subjective call.
overview.why_it_matters: Subjective grading creates disputes and inconsistency across procurement centers, which directly affects farmer payments. A consistent, camera-based grading system makes the process fairer and faster.
pain_points: Quality grading is subjective and inconsistent across different procurement centers.
Inconsistency leads to disputes between farmers and procurement staff.
No standardized, fast, objective grading tool exists at the point of procurement.
overview.background: Onion quality assessment and grading currently varies by inspector and location, creating disputes and inconsistencies that affect farmer payments and procurement fairness.
overview.whats_being_asked: An AI-based mobile app using image processing to assess onion quality, identify damage/rot/sprouting/undersizing, and generate an instant digital quality report.
expected_solution: Image-based quality assessment via mobile app.
Detection of damaged, rotten, sprouted, or undersized onions.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Moderate. Image-based produce quality grading is an established computer-vision application category, the value is in accurate execution for this specific produce type, not a new concept.
analysis.invention_effort_note: Low. A single, well-defined computer vision classification task with a clear, achievable mobile app deliverable, one of the more contained builds in this batch.

competitive_landscape.note: Produce quality-grading via computer vision is a recognizable hackathon problem type, differentiation needs to come from grading accuracy and a genuinely usable field app, not novelty.

innovation.note: Established computer-vision classification pattern, competently applied to a specific, valuable agricultural use case.

invention.note: A single, well-scoped CV classification task, one of the more contained and achievable builds in the batch.

technical_feasibility.note: Onion images are easy to source and label, and CV classification for this kind of visual defect detection is well within reach using existing model architectures.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly reduces procurement disputes and improves fairness, valuable but a narrower, more operational impact than public-health or disaster PS.

architecture.note: Camera input -> classification model -> report output, a straightforward, low-risk pipeline.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick for a team wanting a genuinely low-risk, fully achievable build. Feasibility is comfortable, the deliverable is concrete and demoable, main challenge is execution polish and real-world image variability, not fundamental technical risk.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: One of the most genuinely achievable, low-risk PS in the batch, a real working image classifier with a usable mobile interface is fully within 36-hour reach.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Real onion images vary hugely in lighting, angle, and background, a model trained on clean, uniform sample images will fail on messy real-world procurement-center conditions.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Collect or source varied training/test images (different lighting, angles, backgrounds) rather than a small set of clean, uniform samples, this directly determines real-world usability.

idea_0_4: Source or collect a varied set of onion images spanning good, damaged, rotten, sprouted, and undersized examples.
Choose your classification approach: fine-tuning an existing image classification model is the fastest, most reliable path.
Split: one person on the CV model, one on the mobile app interface.
prototype_4_22: Train/fine-tune your classification model on the varied image set.
Build the mobile camera-capture and classification flow.
Start the grade-percentage calculation and report generation logic.
integration_22_30: Connect capture -> classification -> grading -> report generation end to end.
Test specifically with messy, real-world-style images (poor lighting, cluttered background), not just clean samples.
Add a simple manual-override option for edge cases, this improves real-world trust in the tool.
polish_30_36: Polish the mobile app UI for actual field usability, fast capture, clear results.
Rehearse a live capture-and-grade demo on real onion samples if possible.
Prepare to discuss your model's accuracy honestly, including where it struggles.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Bring real onions to the demo (a mix of good and visibly damaged ones) and grade them live on camera, a real physical demo with real produce is unusually convincing for this kind of PS.

strengths: One of the most genuinely achievable and low-risk PS in the entire batch.
Concrete, real-world demoable deliverable with a physical prop (actual onions) available for the pitch.
weaknesses: Real-world image variability (lighting, background) is the main risk to grading accuracy, needs deliberate attention.
Narrower, more operational impact story than higher-profile PS in the batch.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: CV and mobile-development balanced, this is a contained, well-scoped build that doesn't need a large team.
team_fit.approach: Prioritize image collection/variety early, the model is only as good as the data variety it's trained and tested on.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: The core image classification model (fine-tuning existing architectures is fast and well-supported) and the mobile app scaffold.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Deciding what image variety actually represents real procurement-center conditions, lighting, background clutter, camera angle, that's practical field-testing judgment, not something to assume.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: A model trained only on clean, well-lit sample images will silently fail in real messy field conditions, exactly the gap between a hackathon demo and real deployment.

data_resource_availability.status: Onion images are easy to source (photograph real samples, or use publicly available produce-quality datasets), one of the better-resourced PS in the batch for real data access.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If limited real samples are available, supplement with publicly available produce quality/defect image datasets, and be clear about the mix in your presentation.

judge_qna.question: How does your model perform on real, messy field images, not your clean training samples?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Show your results on a deliberately varied test set (different lighting, background, angle), and be honest about where accuracy drops, that transparency is more credible than a cherry-picked clean-image demo.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your plan for images the model is genuinely uncertain about?

judge_qna.question: How would this actually be adopted at procurement centers, replacing human judgment entirely?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Position it as a consistency and dispute-reduction tool, not a full replacement for human oversight, an inspector can review and override in genuinely ambiguous cases while the app removes the bulk of subjective variability.
judge_qna.follow_up: How do you handle a dispute where the farmer disagrees with the app's grading?
